content.p: The Mongols Motorcycle Club is a Southern California outlaw motorcycle club whose members have been tied, in federal court, to murder, attempted murder, drug trafficking and kidnapping. The club has existed since 1969 and has chapters in several US states and abroad. A US court has also been asked to take away its emblem. Its members and lawyers reject the label of criminal organization, and the courts have given a mixed answer. This account follows the club from its founding to the most recent cases in the sources reviewed.

SlashGear's history says the club began in the late 1960s in east Los Angeles, when a group of Vietnam veterans turned to motorcycles and an outlaw way of life. The same account says established clubs such as the Hells Angels excluded Hispanic and African-American riders, and that this shaped who joined. Founding members incorporated the club in Montebello, California, on 5 December 1969. Their logo was a sketch of Genghis Khan.

In 1974 the club voted to embrace a criminal lifestyle, according to SlashGear. Chapters then spread across California and into neighboring states. The club's growth brought it into the territory of the Hells Angels, which had long dominated California.
content.h2: The feud with the Hells Angels
content.p: The two clubs fought over the methamphetamine trade, according to SlashGear. A brawl at an Anaheim swap meet in 1977 is described as the start of a lasting hostility. On 5 September 1977, returning from a bike run, Emerson Morris, the club's president, and member Raymond Smith were killed in an ambush that SlashGear attributes to Hells Angels. A car bomb later wounded two more Mongols. A series of killings on both sides followed before a truce. Under its terms, the Mongols kept the right to wear the California rocker but were barred from expanding into Northern California, which was Hells Angels territory.
The account is SlashGear's, and the sources reviewed do not describe the 1977 events in more detail. Readers should treat the specific sequence as one published history.

The federal government's case against the Mongols began with an undercover operation. According to the Justice Department's 2019 press release, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives ran the investigation, called Operation Black Rain. Four male agents went undercover and became full-patch members. Four female agents posed as their girlfriends. The release quotes a member telling an agent who had just received his patch: "Being a Mongol promises you one of two things – death or prison."

Individual members were indicted in 2008. NBC News says 77 gang members were convicted of racketeering that year after the agents' work. The Justice Department says 77 members pleaded guilty to violating the RICO statute. Courthouse News reports the 2008 indictment named 79 members and associates, and KFI AM says more than 70 members were convicted. The sources give different counts, and they are not reconciled here.

In 2013 prosecutors filed a case against the club itself. That case was the subject of a long dispute over whether the club could be treated as a criminal enterprise. The defense argued the club was a club, not a gang, that did not tolerate criminal activity, and that the government targeted it because of its large Mexican-American membership. Former Minnesota governor Jesse Ventura, who had been a Mongol in the 1970s, testified for the defense, denying that the Mongols were a criminal gang. Prosecutors described the club as a violent criminal organization.

The trial in Santa Ana, before U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, opened at the end of October 2018. Courthouse News reports that the jury, on 13 December 2018, convicted the Mongol Nation of racketeering and conspiracy to commit racketeering. Courthouse News reports that jurors tied the club to a Los Angeles killing in 2007, an attempted killing in Pasadena in 2008, and drug deals. The Justice Department says the jury found the enterprise responsible for a murder, an attempted murder, a narcotics conspiracy and two methamphetamine transactions. According to Courthouse News, the jury did not prove two other murders or a second attempted murder, and it deadlocked on a third attempted murder. KFI AM describes the non-findings as "not proven" on one attempted murder and two murders, with a 10-2 split.

Prosecutor Steve Welk told the jury that members who commit murder wear a skull-and-crossbones patch as a badge of honor. The defense said the club had ousted its earlier president, Ruben "Doc" Cavazos, for doing things that were inappropriate, and that the alleged crimes happened under his leadership. Stephen Stubbs, the club's general counsel, said: "The Mongols are not a criminal organization and gang."

The second phase of the trial asked a different question: could the government take the club's name and logo? On 11 January 2019, a jury in Santa Ana found that the Mongols' legal interest in the word "Mongols," the center patch, and a combined patch should be forfeited. The Justice Department said this was the first such verdict in the nation. It also covered scores of items with the name and logo seized during the investigation. NBC News reported that a judge still had to approve the forfeiture, and that the practical effect was unclear.

Judge Carter did not order the patch taken. KFI AM reports that he ruled that forfeiting the patch would violate the First and Eighth Amendments. He still fined the club $500,000 and ordered the seizure of ammunition and weapons, according to the same report. Both sides appealed. On 6 January 2023, a three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the refusal to order forfeiture, but on a narrower ground. The panel held that RICO provided no way to forfeit the patch without the government taking title to it. It did not decide the First Amendment question. The panel also upheld the 2018 racketeering conviction and turned down the club's claim that RICO could not be used against it. Stubbs called the ruling a victory for the club. The sources reviewed do not show how the later stages of the appeal ended.

The club's most detailed federal case concerns its Clarksville, Tennessee chapter. The Justice Department says the chapter was set up in early 2015, partly by men who came from another motorcycle club. Their first acts, according to the 2024 release, included attacks on another club's clubhouses in Clarksville and Nashville, which they carried out to win favor with the Mongols. The release says the chapter then operated from 2015 to 2018 as an enterprise engaged in racketeering.

The 2022 release says the chapter kidnapped and murdered Stephanie Bradley in May 2015, after members believed she had information about stolen drugs, money and guns and had been speaking against the club. The 2024 release gives the date as 22 May 2015 and says her body was found almost 15 months later. A second killing, of Stephen Cole, a former member, took place in November 2017. The 2022 release says members believed he had stolen motorcycles belonging to another member.

In September 2022, a federal jury in Nashville convicted six Clarksville men of racketeering conspiracy and related charges, and a seventh man from Kentucky of a drug conspiracy. The 2022 release says the trial covered murder, kidnapping, drug trafficking and money laundering. In April 2024 the Justice Department announced that eighteen members and associates had been federally prosecuted, and that the last of them, James Hines, had been sentenced to 10 years and 10 months. Earlier sentences in the release include life plus 30 years for James Wesley Frazier, 40 years for Aelix Santiago and life plus seven years for William Boylston and Jason Meyerholz. The U.S. Attorney said the case ended "an era of drug-trafficking, violence, and intimidation" in Clarksville.

In March 2025, according to a CBS Los Angeles report of a Justice Department statement, two club members went to a bar in Ontario, California, where a man wearing Vagos Motorcycle Club clothing was attacked. Prosecutors say that one of the men, Julian Pulido, drew a gun when the victim tried to run and fired several times, and that the victim died on the sidewalk outside. Pulido was later located after a chase and was charged with murder in aid of racketeering. The second man, Clifford Michael Lavoy, was charged with assault resulting in serious bodily injury. Both are described in the sources as charged. The sources reviewed do not report a plea or verdict in either case.

In March 2024, a San Bernardino County sheriff's deputy with 18 years of service was arrested after a traffic stop in Beaumont, California, that the San Bernardino Sun reported. The stop followed a surveillance operation. A passenger was wearing a vest with Mongols patches. As the Sun lists the charges, they cover taking a shotgun from the department, gang participation, and weapons that included a machine gun and silencers. The Sun reported he pleaded not guilty on 9 April 2024. The sheriff said the deputy had been placed on compulsory leave. The sources do not establish the full charges or a verdict.
content.h2: Abroad: the New Zealand patch ban
content.p: The club's reach beyond the United States has drawn official action. On 24 April 2020, New Zealand's Police Minister, Stuart Nash, announced that the Mongols Motorcycle Club had been added to the list of gangs whose insignia are banned from government premises. The statement said the New Zealand chapter was likely sparked by members arriving from Australia, and that Australian law enforcement considers the Mongols one of the five worst outlaw motorcycle groups operating across the Tasman. Nash said the ban followed police advice that the club's members share an identifying insignia and promote or engage in crime. The ban applies to government premises. It was the second such insignia he had banned, after Comancheros patches in 2018. These claims are the minister's, and the sources reviewed do not test them independently.

Several figures remain in dispute. Membership estimates vary: NBC News reported more than 1,000 riders in chapters worldwide in 2019, while KFI AM cited law enforcement estimates of about 2,000 full-patched members in 2023. The number of members convicted in the 2008 case is given as 77, more than 70, and a 79-person indictment. The jury's findings on the 2018 murders and attempts also differ slightly between Courthouse News and KFI AM.

The club's lawyers say its members are ordinary people who were penalised for the conduct of a few, and that the club itself is not a criminal enterprise. Prosecutors say the club and its patch are the core of a racketeering enterprise. The courts have found the conviction stood, and that the trademark could not be taken in the form prosecutors asked for. Whether the club will ever be treated differently, and what the appeals will decide, remain open in the sources reviewed.
